science.title: Effect of geometry, wettability, and Janus amphiphilicity on the interfacial attachment strength of peanut-shaped solid particles in Pickering emulsions
science.description: Pickering emulsion are stabilized by solid particles adsorbed at the oil–water interface. The strength of particle interfacial attachment is governed by particle morphology and wettability. This study examines peanut-shaped particles and determine how their geometry and wettability affect particle attachment energy, first as homogeneous particles (uniform wettability) in comparison to the spherical case, and then as Janus particles with one hydrophobic and one hydrophilic face. Homogeneous peanut-shaped particles exhibit more negative attachment energies than a sphere with the same volume, indicating stronger interfacial attachment. To distinguish whether this enhanced attachment arises from the peanut’s larger interfacial contact area or from genuine geometric effects, we compare the peanut against four spherical controls: volume-matched, interfacial-area-matched (cross-section-matched), total-surface-area-matched, and two independent lobe spheres. The results reveal that the peanut’s advantage arises primarily from its larger interfacial contact area, with a smaller but consistent additional contribution from its continuous neck geometry. We then study Janus peanut-shaped particles, where the hydrophobic–hydrophilic boundary is defined by an angle $$\alpha $$, and the wettability contrast $$\beta $$ quantifies the amount by which both face contact angles deviate equally from 90°. The angular position of the oil–water interface $${\alpha}_{v}$$ is then obtained from the minimum free energy. Pinning occurs if, at the minimum energy state, the oil–water interface aligns with this Janus boundary ($${\alpha}_{v}=\alpha $$). For symmetric Janus particles ($$\alpha $$ = 90°), pinning occurs regardless of the wettability contrast between the two faces. However, for asymmetric particles ($$\alpha $$ ≠ 90°), pinning happens only when the wettability contrast exceeds a critical value $${\beta}_{c}$$. The more asymmetric the particle (the farther $$\alpha $$ is from 90°), the larger $${\beta}_{c}$$ must be. Importantly, peanut-shaped Janus particles require a higher $${\beta}_{c}$$ than spherical Janus particles with the same $$\alpha $$. This shows that elongation not only strengthens attachment, but also requires a larger wettability contrast to achieve the pinned configuration. Together these two effects highlight peanut-shaped Janus particles as promising candidates for stronger interfacial attachment in Pickering emulsion applications.

science.title: Radiological and stochastic risk assessments of natural radionuclides in soils of selected hospital waste sites in Anambra State, southeastern Nigeria
science.description: The study focused on measuring radionuclides in 52 soil samples collected around three hospital dumpsites in Anambra State using gamma-ray spectrometry and assessing the associated radiological risks. The average activity concentrations (Bq/kg) of the natural occurring radionuclides (226Ra, 232Th, and 40K) in soils of ANA1 (39.02 ± 18.97, 44.71 ± 23.52, and 72.97 ± 54.18), ANA2 (45.42 ± 21.10, 54.52 ± 26.52, and 140.74 ± 67.51), and ANA3 (52.10 ± 26.16, 66.73 ± 30.03, and 157.55 ± 86.64) were above global recommended averages for 226Ra and 232Th, with more than 60% of the samples having their concentrations above global averages. The radiological effects (average) indicated that the absorbed dose rate for ANA2 and ANA3 was above the threshold; the Representative Level Index and Excess Lifetime Cancer Risks for the study areas were high, close to their permissible values; and the Annual Gonadal Equivalent Doses for the study areas were above the recommended value. Other estimated radiological indices were within their acceptable limits. The statistical analyses showed high variability and heterogeneous spatial patterns, with near-normal distributions, suggesting anthropogenicity influenced concentrations. Stochastic risk assessments using Monte Carlo simulation revealed high risks of cancer effects over long-term exposure. The study reinforced concerns about radiation exposure near hospital waste sites and the urgent need to develop effective mitigation strategies to reduce risks.

science.title: Combined prognostic value of age at onset and socioeconomic status for long-term survival in metastatic breast cancer
science.description: We investigated the combined long-term prognostic value of age at onset and socioeconomic status (SES) on breast cancer overall survival (OS) and metastasis-free survival (MFS) in a cohort of women with metastatic breast cancer. Age at onset was defined as the age at primary diagnosis, with a 40-year cutoff to distinguish early- and late-onset. We estimated individual SES from patients’ reported household income, occupational categories, and education levels. We estimated Kaplan‒Meier survival curves and performed regression analyses using the Cox model, including an interaction term of age at onset and SES. In 109 women included in the study, those with early-onset breast cancer had a non-significantly higher mortality rate than those with late-onset breast cancer (rate difference 0.03/PY). The hazard of metastasis was significantly lower for the medium SES (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.19–0.69) and the high SES (HR 0.34, 95% CI 0.18–0.63) than for the low SES group. Compared to late-onset, early-onset cases had no difference in OS or MFS within the first 10 and 2 years following primary diagnosis, respectively. However, early-onset cases had a worse prognosis thereafter. Similarly, high SES was associated with better survival but only after 7.5 and 3 years following primary diagnosis for OS and MFS, respectively. We found a significant effect modification: higher SES mitigates the effect of early-onset status while it offered minimal survival benefit when age at onset was over 65 years. The combination of age at onset and SES may provide long-term prognostic information. As breast cancer survival has improved in recent decades, addressing SES-related social determinants in clinical settings has become increasingly important for optimizing long-term outcomes.

science.title: Texture attention-guided adaptive LSB steganography with U-Net model and optional GA tuning integrated with ablation study
science.description: Image steganography involves hiding a secret image within a digital cover image, which remains invisible to ordinary viewers. The majority of current steganographic methods face an essential trade-off because higher Payload Capacity (PC) results in decreased visual undetectability and reduced resistance to detection and image distortions. Our proposed framework extracts the texture maps from the cover images, then generates the attention maps, and optionally uses Genetic Algorithm (GA) optimization to achieve maximum imperceptibility and robustness using content-adaptive and texture attention-guided methods. The system generates attention maps through the combination of deep texture maps extracted using ResNet50 blocks with distance transform maps, and then trains a U-Net model to predict these maps for new, unseen cover images. These attention maps guide adaptive bit allocation between 1 and 4 Bits Per Pixel (BPP). Next, we use the GA to optimize both attention threshold values and bit-allocation parameters, which enhances visual quality. The experimental results show that the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) values for all stego-images are between 55 dB and 61 dB. The corresponding Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) values are close to 1.0. Moreover, our framework supports lossless recovery of secret messages embedded in stego-images. The Bit Error Rate (BER) between embedded secret messages and extracted secret messages is equal to 0. The corresponding SSIM values are equal to 1.0. To improve the embedding quality, we employ the GA to search for the optimal values of attention thresholds and adaptive bit allocation. The PSNR improvement of GA-based embedding for stego-images over attention-only embedding for stego-images is approximately 3.6–5.0 dB. Then, we conduct a series of ablation studies to evaluate the contributions of the attention predictor, i.e., a U-Net-based attention predictor, and the GA-based optimization for stego-images of high quality. The results demonstrate that both the attention predictor and the GA-based optimization are necessary to generate stego-images of high quality. We also conduct a computational analysis for embedding and extraction, and the results indicate that both embedding and extraction require only a few milliseconds per image after the one-time offline GA calibration. Finally, we conduct a security evaluation using three state-of-the-art Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based steganalyzers, i.e., Xu-Net, Ye-Net, and SR-Net, for stego-images generated by our framework. The detection performance of the three steganalyzers for stego-images generated by our framework is close to random guessing. The average Area Under the Curve (AUC) values for stego-images generated by our framework are approximately equal to 0.5.
